article.scope_note: Scope reading: this article covers the fluxgate sensing technology itself: how a fluxgate sensor works, and how it has been built into flown lunar surface, lunar orbital and planetary instruments. The generic magnetometer class is payload 012 (Magnetometer). The vector and scalar measurement types are payloads 014 (Vector magnetometer) and 015 (Scalar magnetometer). Those payloads are cross-referenced here, not repeated. An instrument is included as a fluxgate example only where the source identifies its sensor as a fluxgate.
article.overview:
A fluxgate magnetometer measures the strength and direction of a magnetic field by driving a soft magnetic core in and out of magnetic saturation with an alternating current. An external field shifts this cycle, and the shift is read electronically [1][2]. Because the reading depends on the field's component along the sensor axis, fluxgates are used as vector sensors when three are combined on orthogonal axes [2].

The Apollo programme flew fluxgate instruments on the lunar surface and in lunar orbit. The Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Magnetometer is described in the Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report as the first magnetometer operated on the lunar surface [3]. Apollo 14 carried a portable fluxgate instrument [4], and Apollo 15 flew both a surface magnetometer and a subsatellite magnetometer [5]. Later lunar orbiters and planetary missions have used fluxgate magnetometers as well, including Kaguya, Lunar Prospector and MAVEN [2][6][7][8].
article.description:
In an instrument, the fluxgate sensor is connected to electronics and a power supply and is mounted on a boom, tripod or other structure. The sensor is a small coil assembly wound around a magnetically soft core. The core is easily magnetised, and it reaches saturation in each drive cycle. A fluxgate does not measure a field by counting particles or by using atomic transitions. It works by detecting how the magnetisation of its core changes in response to the surrounding field [1][2].

Apollo instruments show how this arrangement was built in practice. The Apollo 14 Lunar Portable Magnetometer used three orthogonal fluxgate sensors on a tripod, connected by a 15 m ribbon cable to an electronics box [4]. The Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Magnetometer placed its three fluxgate sensors at the ends of three 100 cm booms, 75 cm above the surface [5]. The Apollo 15 subsatellite carried two fluxgate sensors at the end of a 1.83 m boom [5].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
Fluxgate magnetometers measure magnetic fields, which can come from several sources. At the Moon these include the Moon's own remanent (crustal) magnetisation, fields generated by the interaction between the solar wind and the lunar surface, and the spacecraft's own magnetic field. A fluxgate on a lunar surface or lunar orbit can help to separate these components.

The Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report states that a permanent magnetic field of 36 gammas and a gradient of 4 × 10⁻³ gammas per cm were measured at the Apollo 12 site [3]. The report also states that the gradient implies a local magnetic body of at least 0.2 km in size [3]. The Apollo 15 subsatellite data were analysed for remanent magnetisation. Preliminary analysis reported fine structure in the field associated with several large craters, including Hertzsprung, Korolev and Gagarin [5]. The report describes detailed mapping as "entirely feasible" with the present experiment [5]. These are preliminary results in the 1972 reports, not final scientific conclusions.

Planetary missions use fluxgates to measure the magnetic fields around other bodies. MAVEN used fluxgate sensors to study the Mars magnetic environment and its interaction with the solar wind [2][6]. Lunar Prospector and Kaguya carried fluxgates in lunar orbit [7][8].
article.operating_principle:
A fluxgate sensor contains a soft ferromagnetic core, usually a Permalloy alloy, wound with a drive coil and a sense coil. A strong alternating current in the drive coil induces an alternating magnetic field in the core and drives it periodically into saturation. With no external field, the sense-coil current matches the drive current. An external field biases the saturation of the core in one direction, which creates an imbalance between the drive and sense signals. That imbalance is proportional to the external field component along the sensor axis [2].

The review cited here gives typical fluxgate performance of about 10 pT per root-Hz sensitivity, a DC resolution of about 5 pT and a spatial resolution of about 10 mm. The review attributes the sensitivity limit to Barkhausen noise in the core and to 1/f noise at low frequencies [2]. These are general values for the technology, not for any specific flown instrument.

The Apollo instruments used different drive schemes. The Apollo 14 Lunar Portable Magnetometer drove its toroidal Permalloy core with a square wave at 7250 Hz, which modulates the core's permeability at twice the drive frequency [4]. The Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Magnetometer drove its sensors with a sinusoidal current at 6000 Hz [5]. In the Apollo 15 instrument, the sense winding detects the combined field of the drive winding and the total lunar-surface field [5].

Calibration is a part of the operating principle. The Apollo 15 magnetometer applied internal calibration biases in steps of 0, ±25, ±50 and ±75 per cent of full scale. The sequence was repeated every 18 hours by timer command [5].
article.scientific_importance:
Fluxgate magnetometers provide direct field measurements that other instruments cannot supply. Seismometers, for example, record seismic waves but not magnetic fields. A fluxgate on the Moon or in lunar orbit adds a complementary view of the crust and its environment.

The Apollo results show what a fluxgate can measure on the lunar surface. The Apollo 12 measurements gave a permanent field and gradient for one site [3]. The Apollo 14 portable instrument, which was moved by the astronauts, reported surface fields in the range of 40 to 100 gammas at two separate sites [4]. These measurements helped to establish the lunar surface magnetic environment during the Apollo era.

The later orbital instruments extend this work to other bodies. The Kaguya and Lunar Prospector data show how a fluxgate can map crustal fields from orbit [7][8]. MAVEN applied fluxgates to Mars [6]. The orbital and planetary records are not directly comparable with the surface instruments, because the measurement geometry, sensor placement and calibration differ.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, power or sensitivity for a fluxgate magnetometer. A fluxgate can be a single-axis sensor, a three-axis sensor or a gradiometer pair, and the electronics and boom design vary by mission. The examples below are named instruments. Each value is tied to its source. Where a value is not stated in the sources read, the article says so. The Apollo 14 and Apollo 15 table values were read from OCR text and should be checked against the scanned pages before reuse.

examples.name: Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Magnetometer
examples.description: The Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Magnetometer was described as a "very sophisticated three-component fluxgate instrument" [3]. It was part of the Apollo 12 ALSEP package [4]. The report gives a measured permanent field of 36 gammas and a gradient of 4 × 10⁻³ gammas per cm [3]. Mass, dimensions, power and sensitivity are not stated in the report sections read, so they are not given here.

examples.name: Apollo 14 Lunar Portable Magnetometer (LPM)
examples.status: Flown (lunar surface, portable; carried on the lunar module and the Modularized Equipment Transporter)
examples.description:
The Apollo 14 Lunar Portable Magnetometer (LPM) was carried on the lunar module and then on the Modularized Equipment Transporter. On the surface it was deployed on a tripod with three orthogonal fluxgate sensors. The sensors were connected by a 15 m ribbon cable to an electronics box that contained the battery pack, electronics and three milliammeters [4]. Each sensor weighs 18 g and uses 15 mW in operation [4]. The sensor core is a flattened toroidal Permalloy core driven by a 7250 Hz square wave [4]. The instrument was aligned using a bubble level and a shadowgraph, with alignment along the Moon-Sun line [4].

The report's Table 13-1 lists the LPM characteristics. The OCR text of that table is garbled, so the value-to-label mapping below is inferred from the order of the rows and should be checked against the scanned page. The listed values are: field ranges of 0 to ±100 and 0 to ±50 gammas; resolutions of ±1.0 and ±0.5 gammas; battery power 1.5 W; battery life 60 hours; mass 4.58 kg; stowage size 55.9 × 15.3 × 14.3 cm; and an operating temperature of −30 °C to +60 °C [4].

Figure 13-3 of the Apollo 14 report shows the LPM on the Modularized Equipment Transporter and deployed at site A during the measurement of a 103-gamma field [4]. The figure is cited as a linked reference only (see the images below).

examples.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Magnetometer
examples.type: Lunar surface fluxgate magnetometer (ALSEP central station)
examples.description:
The Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Magnetometer had three orthogonal fluxgate sensors. They were located at the ends of three 100 cm orthogonal booms, separated from each other by 150 cm and 75 cm above the lunar surface [5]. Each sensor has a Permalloy toroidal core driven at 6000 Hz [5]. Orientation was measured with a shadowgraph and bubble level [5].

Table 9-I of the Apollo 15 report lists the instrument characteristics. The table was read from OCR, so the values should be checked against the scanned page. The listed values are: field ranges of 0 to ±200, 0 to ±100 and 0 to ±50 gammas, with the "solar-wind plasma" label placed beside the first range; a resolution of ±0.1 gamma; frequency response from DC to 3 Hz; average power of 3.5 W in daytime and 9.4 W at night; mass of 8.9 kg; size of 25 × 28 × 63 cm; and operating temperature from −50 °C to +85 °C [5]. The table also lists a sensor geometry of three orthogonal sensors on 100 cm booms and a modes list that includes orthogonal field measurement, gradient measurement and internal calibration [5].
examples.sensor_configuration: Three orthogonal fluxgate sensors at the ends of three 100 cm booms, separated by 150 cm and 75 cm above the lunar surface.
examples.core_and_drive: Flattened toroidal Permalloy core driven to saturation by a sinusoidal current at 6000 Hz.
ranges_gamma: 0 to ±200 (table places 'solar-wind plasma' beside this range)
examples.internal_calibration: Bias steps of 0, ±25, ±50 and ±75 per cent of full scale; sequence repeated every 18 hours by timer command.
examples.orientation: Shadowgraph and bubble level used to relate the sensors to lunar coordinates.
examples.modes_of_operation: Orthogonal field measurements, gradient measurement, internal calibration (Table 9-I OCR).

examples.name: Kaguya (SELENE) Lunar Magnetometer (LMAG)
examples.description: The Kaguya LMAG sensor was mounted on the edge of a super-lightweight mast extended 12 m from the spacecraft [7]. The ODE instrument page does not state the sensor type, the number of sensors, mass, power or the operating dates [7]. The page says the instrument can measure a magnetic field weaker than 1/100,000 of the geomagnetic field, and gives a calibrated sampling interval of four seconds [7]. A search summary of other Kaguya papers describes a triaxial ring-core fluxgate sensor (MGF-S). That description was not verified in full text and is not used as a specification here.
examples.sensor_configuration: Sensor mounted on the edge of a super-lightweight mast extended 12 m from the spacecraft (ODE page). Sensor type and count not stated on the ODE page.
examples.sensitivity_statement: Can measure a magnetic field weaker than 1/100,000 of the geomagnetic field (ODE page; no absolute nT value given).
examples.unverified_summary: A search summary of other Kaguya papers describes a triaxial ring-core fluxgate sensor (MGF-S). Not verified in full text and not used as a specification.

examples.name: Lunar Prospector magnetometer (MAG)
examples.description: The ODE instrument page describes the Lunar Prospector MAG as "a 3-axis fluxgate magnetometer and an electronics box", with one magnetometer sensor [8]. The page gives a wide measurement range of up to ±65,536 nT, a low noise of 6 pT RMS, and a sensitivity as low as ±2 pT [8]. The boom length, native sample rate and mission dates are not stated on that page [8]. Other summaries give a boom of about 2.5 m, and the Goddard instrument summary describes a dual sensor system. These conflict with the ODE description and are not used as specifications [8].
examples.sensor_configuration: 'a 3-axis fluxgate magnetometer and an electronics box' with one magnetometer sensor (ODE page).
examples.measurement_range_nt: Wide range up to ±65,536 nT (ODE page)
examples.conflicts: A Goddard summary describes a dual sensor system, and other summaries give a boom of about 2.5 m. These conflict with the ODE page and are not used as specifications.

examples.name: MAVEN Magnetometer (MAG)
examples.status: Flown (Mars orbit; launched 18 November 2013, orbit entry 21 September 2014)
examples.description: The MAVEN magnetometers are described as triaxial fluxgate instruments (FGM). They were mounted on "boomlets" at either end of the deployable solar-array panels, not on a dedicated magnetometer boom [2][6]. MAVEN was launched on 18 November 2013 and entered Mars orbit on 21 September 2014 [2]. The review's table lists a MAVEN FGM range of ±512, but the units and column meaning were not confirmed in the extracted text. The paper abstract summary gives a dynamic range of 65,536 nT per axis and a sample rate of 32 vectors per second. Those abstract details were not read from the full paper and are not used as specifications here [6].
examples.sensor_configuration: Triaxial fluxgate (FGM) sensors mounted on boomlets at either end of the deployable solar-array panels, not on a dedicated boom. Two sensors per the paper abstract summary.
examples.review_table_range: ±512 (review table; units and column meaning not confirmed in the extracted text)

abstract_summary_values.status: From an abstract summary, not from the full paper; not used as specifications

examples.name: Psyche magnetometer (mission design)
examples.type: Planned deep-space fluxgate magnetometer (mission design described in review)
examples.status: Planned mission design as described in a 2021 review; current flight status not verified in this run
examples.description: The 2021 review describes the Psyche magnetometer as two identical fluxgate sensors in a gradiometer configuration, located at the middle and outer end of a magnetometer boom [2]. It reports two selectable dynamic ranges of ±1000 nT and ±10⁵ nT, with resolutions of ±0.1 nT and ±10 pT [2]. The review describes the mission's magnetometer design. The current status of the mission and its instrument was not verified in this run, so the example is treated as a design description only.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Surface instruments are exposed to large temperature changes. The Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Magnetometer is listed with an operating range of −50 °C to +85 °C [5]. The Apollo 14 LPM is listed with −30 °C to +60 °C [4]. These values come from OCR-read tables and should be checked.

The instrument's power draw changes between lunar day and night in the Apollo 15 design. The table gives average power of 3.5 W in daytime and 9.4 W at night [5]. Thermal and power planning for a surface instrument must therefore account for this difference.

Magnetic cleanliness is a practical requirement. The Acuña review states that spacecraft may not be magnetically clean, and that deployable booms can separate sensors from contamination sources [1]. The Apollo 15 instruments used booms, but the report sections read do not state the purpose of each boom [5].

Orientation is an operational requirement. The Apollo 14 and 15 instruments needed alignment to lunar coordinates, using a shadowgraph and a bubble level [4][5]. Without this, the vector components cannot be related to the lunar frame.
article.limitations:
Fluxgate sensitivity is limited by Barkhausen noise in the core and by 1/f noise at low frequencies. The review gives these as the main limits on fluxgate sensitivity [2]. The Acuña review notes a further concern: the decline in availability of Permalloy-family soft magnetic materials may limit the development of high-performance fluxgates [1].

Spacecraft fields are a central limitation. A spacecraft may not be magnetically clean, and its own field can mask the lunar or planetary field [1]. Booms and dual-magnetometer techniques are used to reduce this effect [1].

Surface instruments have an additional limitation. The Apollo 14 LPM had to be aligned in the field with a bubble level and a shadowgraph [4]. The Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Magnetometer sensors were at fixed positions on their booms [5].

Miniaturised magnetoresistive and micromachined sensors have improved, but the Acuña review states that they did not yet meet the accuracy needed for major science missions [1]. A smaller fluxgate can also suffer more from contamination [1].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Surface payloads (Apollo 14 LPM, Apollo 15 LSM) and orbital payloads (Apollo 15 subsatellite, MAVEN) are handled separately. The Apollo 14 LPM was portable and carried on the lunar module and the Modularized Equipment Transporter. The Apollo 15 surface magnetometer was part of the ALSEP central station installation. The Apollo 15 subsatellite was a lunar-orbit payload. MAVEN's sensors are on boomlets at its solar arrays. No lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted for any example.
transportation_process: Surface (Apollo 14 LPM): stowed on the lunar module scientific equipment bay during transit from Earth [4].

Surface (Apollo 14 LPM): carried on the Modularized Equipment Transporter on the lunar surface, then deployed on a tripod with three orthogonal sensors connected by a 15 m ribbon cable to the electronics box [4].
Surface (Apollo 15 LSM): part of the ALSEP central station installation, with three sensors on 100 cm booms [5]. The delivery and set-up sequence was not read.
Orbiter (Apollo 15 subsatellite): two fluxgate sensors on a 1.83 m boom, with the electronics unit housed in the spacecraft [5]. The release and deployment sequence was not read.
Orbiter (MAVEN): sensors on boomlets at the ends of the deployable solar-array panels [2][6].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo 14 LPM: tripod deployment with a 15 m cable and in-field alignment to the Moon-Sun line using a bubble level and shadowgraph [4]. Apollo 15 LSM: fixed sensor positions on three 100 cm orthogonal booms, 75 cm above the surface [5]. Apollo 15 subsatellite: fixed 1.83 m boom with two orthogonal sensors [5]. MAVEN: boomlets on the solar arrays [2]. Apollo 12 deployment method not stated in the sections read.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Magnetometer (1969 mission; report 1970) [3]. Apollo 14 Lunar Portable Magnetometer (1971 report) [4]. Apollo 15 Lunar Surface Magnetometer and Particles and Fields Subsatellite Magnetometer (1972 report) [5]. MAVEN (launched 18 November 2013; Mars orbit from 21 September 2014) [2].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Not assessed. No named lander, rover or spacecraft interface was verified for any fluxgate example in this article. The sources describe mission-specific accommodation only.

article.historical_significance:
The Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Magnetometer was the first magnetometer operated on the lunar surface, according to the Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report [3]. The Apollo 14 Lunar Portable Magnetometer extended this capability to a portable, astronaut-deployed instrument [4]. The Apollo 15 surface and subsatellite magnetometers showed that fluxgate data could be combined across the lunar surface and orbit [5].

Later orbital and planetary missions used fluxgate magnetometers for lunar and planetary mapping. Lunar Prospector, Kaguya, MAVEN and the Psyche mission design all rely on this technology [2][6][7][8]. The 2021 review describes heritage fluxgate magnetometers as widely used in space [2], and the Acuña review notes the materials concern discussed above [1].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: OCR-derived tables. The Apollo 14 LPM Table 13-1 and the Apollo 15 LSM Table 9-I were read from OCR text. The Apollo 14 label-to-value mapping is inferred from the row order. These values should be checked against the scanned pages. Apollo 12 specifications. Mass, dimensions, power and sensitivity for the Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Magnetometer were not found in the report sections read. Apollo 15 subsatellite specifications. Mass, power, sensor dimensions and the release sequence were not found in the sections read. Kaguya LMAG. The ODE page does not state the sensor type, the sensor count, mass, power or operating dates. The triaxial ring-core description comes from a search summary and was not verified in full text. Lunar Prospector MAG. The ODE page describes one sensor, but a Goddard summary describes a dual system. Boom length is conflicting in the search summaries and is not verified. MAVEN. The review table lists a range of ±512, while the abstract summary gives 65,536 nT per axis. The full MAVEN paper [6] was not read. Psyche. Status and design details come from a 2021 review. They were not checked against current mission documentation. Apollo 16. The Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report (NTRS 19730013002) contains many magnetometer mentions, including the lunar portable magnetometer. It was not analysed for this article. Juno. The Juno magnetometer is mentioned in the 2021 review, but its specifications were not read. Images. One direct image asset was verified: the NASA Apollo 15 mini-panorama. No direct image asset was verified for the Apollo 14 LPM figure, so it is cited as a linked reference only. DOI access. The Acuña (2002) DOI returned HTTP 403 to curl. Bibliographic details were confirmed from the AIP landing page, but the full text was not read.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values, and all reference URLs, have query strings and fragments removed. Direct image URL https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/a15pan11845-7.jpg returned HTTP 200 image/jpeg on 2026-11-12 (curl). Source pages and reference URLs returned HTTP 200 to curl on the same date, except the Acuña reference (DOI 10.1063/1.1510570 and its AIP landing page both return HTTP 403 to curl; the AIP page was read through the reader instead).

data_quality_notes: Scope: this article reads the payload as the fluxgate sensing technology and its instrument implementations. Payloads 012 (Magnetometer), 014 (Vector magnetometer) and 015 (Scalar magnetometer) are cross-referenced, not repeated.

Apollo 14 LPM Table 13-1 is OCR-garbled. The label-to-value mapping (battery power 1.5 W, life 60 hr, mass 4.58 kg, stowage size, operating temperature, ranges and resolutions) is inferred from row order and must be checked against the scanned page.

Apollo 15 LSM Table 9-I was read from OCR. Values (ranges 0 to ±200, ±100, ±50 gamma; resolution ±0.1 gamma; DC to 3 Hz; 3.5 W day and 9.4 W night average; 8.9 kg; 25 x 28 x 63 cm; -50 to +85 °C) should be checked against the scanned page. The 'solar-wind plasma' label placement is unclear in the OCR.
Apollo 12 LSM: mass, dimensions, power and sensitivity not stated in the report sections read. The 36-gamma field and the 4 x 10^-3 gamma/cm gradient are as printed in OCR text.
Apollo 15 subsatellite magnetometer: mass, power, sensor dimensions and release sequence not stated in the sections read.

Kaguya LMAG: ODE page does not state sensor type, sensor count, mass, power or operating dates. The triaxial ring-core (MGF-S) description comes from a search summary and is not verified in full text. The sensitivity statement is qualitative only.

Lunar Prospector MAG: ODE page describes one sensor. A Goddard summary describes a dual system, and other summaries give a boom of about 2.5 m; these conflict with the ODE page and are not used. Mission dates and native sample rate not verified.

MAVEN: the review table lists a range of ±512 (units and column unconfirmed), while the abstract summary gives 65,536 nT per axis and 32 vector samples per second. The full Connerney et al. (2015) paper was not read, so these values are not used as specifications.
Psyche: design details come from the 2021 review only. Current mission status and instrument specifications were not checked against current mission documentation.
Acuña (2002): DOI 10.1063/1.1510570 is confirmed by the AIP landing page. The DOI URL returns HTTP 403 to curl. Only the abstract summary was read; the full text was not read.

Fluxgate principle and performance (about 10 pT per root-Hz sensitivity, DC resolution about 5 pT, spatial resolution about 10 mm, Barkhausen and 1/f noise limits) are general values from the 2021 review, not for a named flown instrument.

Apollo 14 LPM and Apollo 15 LSM design values (drive frequencies 7250 Hz and 6000 Hz; Permalloy toroidal cores) are from the report text. The Apollo 16 subsatellite and other Apollo 16 magnetometer material (NTRS 19730013002) contains many magnetometer mentions but was not analysed for this article.

Images: one direct image asset was verified (NASA Apollo 15 mini-panorama, AS15-11845/11847). The Apollo 14 LPM Figure 13-3 has no verified direct asset and is cited as a linked reference only (image_url null). No sensor-level photograph of a fluxgate instrument was verified for the other examples.
Juno magnetometer is mentioned in the 2021 review but its specifications were not read and it is not analysed as an example.
No lunar landing-site or location recommendation is included, in line with the deferral by the user. No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted.
